[batch narration moved out of reading 2026-09-02] CyrusOne was founded in July 2000 by David Ferdman and Larry Bursten, who had previously built companies acquired by IXC Communications. The company was purchased by Cincinnati Bell for 525 million dollars in 2010, completed an IPO in 2013, and was taken private again in 2022 when Kohlberg Kravis Roberts and Global Infrastructure Partners acquired it for 15 billion dollars. Sourcing fetched this session gave detailed acquisition stories for several CyrusOne markets, including Texas, Virginia, Ohio, Arizona, Illinois, and Connecticut, but did not contain a specific opening date, investment figure, or building history for this particular state cluster. No building specific address or individual MW figures were located in available sourcing this session.

reading.body:
CyrusOne Council Bluffs, IA (OCB1) in Council Bluffs, Iowa, publishes 9 MW of IT capacity across 420,000 square feet of technical space, operated by CyrusOne.

At 10 kW per rack, a common enterprise colocation density, that load supports roughly 900 racks. At 40 kW per rack, a density closer to AI training workloads, it supports roughly 225 racks. The operator has not published a per-rack power envelope, so neither figure is the operator's own claim, only what the published megawattage implies under each assumption.

CyrusOne Council Bluffs, IA (OCB1) holds 5 published certifications: PCI DSS (the standard required to handle payment card data), HIPAA (handling of protected health information), FISMA (a specific compliance or security standard), TIA-942 (a specific compliance or security standard), HITRUST (a healthcare-focused security framework built on top of HIPAA). Together these qualify the facility for regulated workloads spanning security auditing, payments, and healthcare data, though which specific tenants rely on which certification is not disclosed.

Iowa has 2 facilities mapped in this site's dataset, of which 2 publish a megawatt figure, totaling 18 MW. CyrusOne Council Bluffs, IA (OCB1) contributes 9 MW of that total. At that published size it is a small facility relative to what frontier AI training infrastructure requires, which now runs into the tens or hundreds of megawatts, though it may still support inference workloads or smaller-scale AI applications.
